title: CT thorax — axial through the heart
summary: The chest radiograph's silhouettes, pulled apart into one slice.
text:
The same chest as the plain film, cut across just above the diaphragm. Everything the radiograph could only show as an overlapping outline is now separate: the heart sits in the middle, lung is black on both sides, and the descending aorta and oesophagus lie in front of the vertebral body.

Compare the two: on the film the left heart border is one continuous line, and here you can see it is the left ventricle with lung packed against it. Lose the air in that lung and the line goes – which is the whole basis of the silhouette sign.

Patient's right on your left, anterior at the top. The 3D view beside it is cut in the same plane at the same level.
reading: Orientation first: patient's right on your left, anterior up.
Then compartments, not eye-catching abnormalities: lungs, pleura, mediastinum (heart, great vessels, oesophagus), body wall, bones.
Normal lung on a soft-tissue window is black apart from vessels, which taper as they run outwards. Anything else in it is abnormal.
Follow the descending aorta through consecutive slices: its calibre, its wall and whether there is any fluid or blood beside it.
Finally the bones on a bone window, and the body wall – rib fractures and surgical emphysema hide in plain sight on a soft-tissue window.

title: CT head — axial, non-contrast
summary: The first scan in a head injury, and the four densities you are looking for.
text:
A plain CT head: no contrast, because the question is blood, and fresh blood is already bright (50–80 HU) against grey matter (about 40) and white matter (about 30).

The slice is angled, so it passes through the frontal sinuses at the front and the atria of the lateral ventricles at the back – you can see the little calcified lumps of choroid plexus in them, a normal finding after about the age of twenty.

Bone is white and swamps the window, so the same slice is always reviewed twice: once on brain settings and once on bone settings.
reading: Blood: look at the places it collects – extradural (lens-shaped, does not cross sutures), subdural (crescent, crosses sutures), subarachnoid (in the sulci and cisterns), intraparenchymal, intraventricular.
Then symmetry: the midline structures central, the ventricles equal, the sulci the same on both sides.
Then the cisterns – especially the basal cisterns; effaced cisterns mean raised intracranial pressure.
Grey–white differentiation: loss of it is an early infarct.
Finally the bones and the sinuses on a bone window – a skull fracture, or blood in a sinus as the only clue to a base-of-skull injury.

title: MRI brain — axial T2
summary: Water is bright. That one rule organises the whole image.
text:
On a T2-weighted image, water is bright: CSF in the ventricles and sulci glows, so does oedema, and so does almost every acute pathology. Fat is fairly bright, and flowing blood in a vessel is black. On T1 the contrast is reversed – CSF dark, fat bright – which is why both are always acquired.

This slice cuts through the basal ganglia and thalami, the most useful axial level in the brain: you can see the frontal horns, the caudate heads, the lentiform nuclei, the internal capsules between them and the thalami behind.

Patient's right on your left, anterior at the top.
reading: Establish the sequence before anything else: bright CSF means T2, dark CSF means T1. Then find the abnormality's signal relative to normal brain.
Work through the deep grey matter in order: caudate, lentiform, internal capsule, thalamus – strokes and metabolic diseases pick these out with characteristic patterns.
The ventricles and cisterns: size, symmetry, and whether the quadrigeminal cistern still smiles.
The cortex and subcortical white matter, comparing left with right region by region.
Vessels are black; a bright vessel means slow or absent flow. Check the dural sinuses for the same reason.

title: MRI knee — sagittal
summary: Everything the radiograph could not show: ligament, cartilage, tendon, fat pad.
text:
A sagittal slice through the intercondylar region, anterior to the left. The two arrows on the original image mark the cruciate ligaments – the reason MRI replaced arthrography for the knee.

The anterior cruciate runs from the back of the lateral femoral condyle downwards and forwards to the front of the tibia; it stops the tibia sliding forwards, and it should be a straight dark band parallel to Blumensaat's line. The posterior cruciate is thicker and arcs backwards to the posterior tibia; it stops the tibia sliding backwards.

Note what the plain lateral film of the same joint could not show you at all: cartilage, ligament, the fat pad, and the popliteal vessels behind.
reading: Find the sequence, then the ACL on the sagittal slices through the notch – a straight, taut, dark band. A wavy or absent band, or fluid in its place, is a tear.
The PCL is normally a thick dark arc; it only ruptures in high-energy injury, so a PCL tear means looking hard for other damage.
Menisci on the peripheral sagittal slices: dark bow ties. Any bright line reaching an articular surface is a tear.
Articular cartilage on both femoral condyles and the patella, then the subchondral bone for marrow oedema – the bone bruise that tells you where the impact was.
Finally the extensor mechanism, collateral ligaments on the coronals, and the popliteal fossa.
